lead: This unit is about property data: how a pure substance changes phase, how steam tables and the Mollier chart give h, s and v, and how gas mixtures are described. After it, a student can fix the state of water or steam, compute dryness fraction and mixture properties, use the compressibility chart, and read a psychrometric chart.
about: This unit supplies the property data that every steam and gas calculation needs. Chapter 5.1 shows phase change of a pure substance on p-v-T coordinates, and 5.2 fixes the triple and critical points. 5.3 counts the free properties with the Gibbs phase rule. 5.4 builds steam properties from latent heat and dryness fraction; 5.5 reads steam tables and the Mollier chart; 5.6 measures dryness with calorimeters. 5.7 compares ideal and real gas equations of state, 5.8 corrects them with the compressibility factor and chart, 5.9 applies Dalton’s and Amagat’s laws to gas mixtures, and 5.10 uses humidity and the psychrometric chart for moist air.

chapters.idea: A pure substance at fixed composition passes through compressed liquid, saturated liquid, wet mixture, saturated vapour and superheated vapour states; p-v-T surfaces collect these states.
chapters.depth: Define pure substance, phase, saturation, subcooled or compressed liquid, wet mixture, superheated vapour, and quality x. Show constant-pressure heating on T-v and p-v planes; describe the p-v-T surface and the triple line. Some syllabi call the wet region the saturation dome. Use water as the example; mention ice-water-vapour. Keep to property behaviour.

figure.title: Constant-pressure heating of water
figure.aria: Five boxes in a row show water heated at constant pressure from compressed liquid to saturated liquid, wet mixture, saturated vapour and superheated vapour.

chapters.example: 2 kg of water at 101.325 kPa has dryness fraction x = 0.25. At this pressure v_f = 0.001043 m³/kg and v_g = 1.694 m³/kg. Find the total volume and the mass of liquid and vapour.
chapters.trap: Treating a wet mixture as one phase and using v_g when x is not 1. Dryness fraction multiplies the latent part, not the whole specific volume.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: system, property, state; specific volume as an intensive property.
chapters.leave: Steam table readings and interpolations go to 5.5; entropy changes and T-s diagrams go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Triple point is the only state where solid, liquid and vapour coexist; critical point ends the liquid-vapour saturation curve.
chapters.depth: Use p-T and p-v diagrams. State triple-point values for water: 273.16 K, 0.6117 kPa. Critical values: 647.1 K, 22.064 MPa. Explain sublimation below triple pressure, melting, vaporisation, and why liquid and vapour become indistinguishable above critical. Mention the critical isotherm on a p-v diagram. Some syllabi call critical state the critical point.

figure.aria: A plot of log pressure against temperature shows the sublimation line meeting the vaporisation line at the triple point and the vaporisation line ending at the critical point.

chapters.example: For water, the triple point is 273.16 K and 0.6117 kPa; the critical point is 647.1 K and 22.064 MPa. A sample is held at 0.5 kPa and 0°C. Is liquid water stable? What happens on slow heating? Answer: pressure is below triple pressure, so ice sublimes; liquid is not stable.
chapters.trap: Reading 0.6117 kPa as 0.6117 MPa or using gauge pressure; above critical pressure a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone at that temperature.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 phase names and saturation; Unit 1 equilibrium and property diagrams.
chapters.leave: Clausius-Clapeyron equation and slope of phase boundaries go to Unit 4; steam table values go to 5.5.

chapters.idea: F = C − P + 2 counts the free intensive properties of a system in equilibrium.
chapters.depth: Components, phases, degrees of freedom; derivation by counting; pure substance and moist air.

chapters.idea: At constant pressure, water absorbs sensible heat to saturation, latent heat while boiling, and sensible heat again when superheated; dryness fraction fixes the position inside the wet region.
chapters.depth: Define h_f, h_g, h_fg = h_g - h_f, x = m_g/(m_f+m_g), and h = h_f + x h_fg; give v and s by the same rule. Use T-v, T-h and h-s sketches. Show latent heat decreasing to zero at the critical point. Use water at 1 atm and 10 bar. Some syllabi call x quality. Keep to steam formation, not cycle analysis.

figure.aria: A temperature-enthalpy plot at 1 atm rises from 20 to 100 degrees Celsius, stays flat during boiling from 419 to 2676 kilojoules per kilogram, then rises again in superheated steam.

chapters.example: 2 kg of wet steam at 1 atm has dryness fraction 0.9. At 1 atm h_f = 419 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg. Find h, total enthalpy, and the mass of liquid and vapour. Answer: h = 2450.3 kJ/kg, H = 4900.6 kJ, m_g = 1.8 kg, m_f = 0.2 kg.
chapters.trap: Adding h_fg once per kilogram when x is not 1, or treating quality as a percentage without dividing by 100.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 wet mixture; Unit 2 enthalpy as u + pv.
chapters.leave: Entropy of wet steam and T-s process paths go to Unit 3; Mollier chart reading to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Steam tables and the Mollier chart turn measured p, T or x into h, v and s without solving equations.
chapters.depth: Show layout of saturated and superheated tables: saturation rows by p or T, superheated rows by p and T. Interpolate only when needed. Read the h-s Mollier chart: saturation dome, constant-pressure, constant-temperature and constant-dryness lines. Use absolute pressure; gauge = absolute - atmospheric. Some syllabi call the chart an h-s diagram. Leave Rankine cycle to Unit 6.

figure.aria: A decision tree uses p and T to choose superheated steam, saturated steam or compressed liquid tables.

chapters.example: Steam at 10 bar absolute and 250°C. Find its state and give h, v and s from the superheated steam table. Answer: T_sat = 179.9°C, so it is superheated; h ≈ 2943 kJ/kg, v ≈ 0.2327 m³/kg, s ≈ 6.925 kJ/kgK.
chapters.trap: Entering a gauge pressure in a steam table, or using the saturated table when T is above T_sat. At 10 bar gauge the absolute pressure is about 11 bar.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 saturation temperature; 5.4 h_f and h_fg; Unit 1 pressure units.
chapters.leave: Rankine cycle, reheat and regeneration go to Unit 6; entropy generation and second law go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A throttling calorimeter finds steam dryness from the temperature after a throttling process, using h before equal to h after.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover the throttling calorimeter and separating calorimeter in outline. For throttling: wet steam at p1 is throttled to p2, T2; if the outlet is superheated, h1 = h2, then x1 = (h2 - h_f1)/h_fg1. Mention limits: outlet must be superheated, and very wet steam needs a separating calorimeter. Do not derive instrument corrections.

figure.title: Throttling calorimeter
figure.aria: A flow diagram of a throttling calorimeter: wet steam at 10 bar passes a throttle, leaves at 1 bar and 130 degrees Celsius superheated, and the dryness fraction 0.979 is calculated from equal enthalpies.

chapters.example: In a throttling calorimeter, wet steam at 10 bar is throttled to 1 bar and 130°C. At 10 bar h_f = 762.6 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2015.3 kJ/kg; at 1 bar and 130°C h = 2736 kJ/kg. Find x1. Answer: x1 = (2736 - 762.6)/2015.3 = 0.979.
chapters.trap: Using h1 = h2 when the outlet is still wet; then the throttling calorimeter is invalid. Also ignore kinetic and potential energy only when changes are small.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 dryness fraction; Unit 2 steady flow energy equation; 5.5 steam tables.
chapters.leave: Full instrument construction and error analysis go to laboratory courses; separating calorimeter details can be a short note.

chapters.idea: Ideal gas obeys pv = RT; real gases deviate near saturation and high pressure, so equations of state add molecular volume and attraction terms.
chapters.depth: State ideal gas assumptions and R = R_u/M. Define compressibility later. Give the van der Waals equation (p + a/v²)(v - b) = RT with each term defined. Mention Redlich-Kwong and Beattie-Bridgeman only by name if listed. Some syllabi call a real gas a non-ideal gas. Do not derive Maxwell relations.

figure.aria: Two pressure-volume curves for one mole of carbon dioxide at 300 kelvin almost overlap: the ideal curve and the van der Waals curve differ slightly near 0.024 cubic metres per mole.

chapters.example: 1 mol of CO2 is held at 300 K in 0.024 m³. Take R = 8.314 J/molK, a = 0.3640 Pa m⁶/mol² and b = 4.267×10⁻⁵ m³/mol. Find p from the ideal gas law and from van der Waals. Answer: ideal p = 103.9 kPa; van der Waals p = 103.5 kPa.
chapters.trap: Using v as total volume in the van der Waals equation; v there is molar volume V/n. Mixing units of a and b with R.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 state and property; Unit 2 pv = RT and specific heats; 5.1 phase change.
chapters.leave: Compressibility chart and reduced properties go to 5.8; Maxwell and Clapeyron relations go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The compressibility factor Z = pv/RT measures how far a real gas is from ideal, and the generalized chart gives Z from reduced pressure and temperature.
chapters.depth: Define p_R = p/p_c, T_R = T/T_c and v_R. Show the Z chart: Z = 1 ideal, curves of constant T_R. Use Z to find v = ZRT/p. Mention the principle of corresponding states. Keep chart reading approximate. Some syllabi call it the generalized compressibility chart.

figure.title: Compressibility chart route
figure.aria: A block diagram takes nitrogen at 10 megapascals and 300 kelvin, forms reduced properties 2.95 and 2.38, reads Z near 1.0, and computes specific volume.

chapters.example: Nitrogen at 300 K and 10 MPa. p_c = 3.39 MPa, T_c = 126.2 K, R = 0.2968 kJ/kgK. Find T_R, p_R, and estimate v using Z from the chart. Answer: T_R = 2.38, p_R = 2.95, Z ≈ 1.0, v = 0.00890 m³/kg.
chapters.trap: Using gauge pressure or Celsius in reduced properties; p_R and T_R need absolute pressure and kelvin.
chapters.leave: Detailed cubic equations of state and fugacity go to advanced thermodynamics; mixture compressibility gets only a mention in 5.9.

chapters.idea: In an ideal gas mixture, each gas behaves as if alone in the same volume (Dalton) or at the same pressure (Amagat); mole fraction sets its share.
chapters.depth: Define mole fraction y_i, mass fraction, partial pressure p_i = y_i p, partial volume V_i = y_i V. Dalton: p = Σp_i. Amagat: V = ΣV_i. Give mixture molar mass M_mix = Σy_iM_i and gas constant R_mix = R_u/M_mix. Use only ideal gas mixtures; real mixture corrections later. Some old notes spell Amagat as Amalgam.

figure.title: n (kmol), y, p (MPa)
figure.aria: A table lists 2 kilomoles of nitrogen and 3 kilomoles of oxygen, their mole fractions 0.4 and 0.6, and Dalton partial pressures 9.98 and 15.0 megapascals, giving 24.9 megapascals total.

chapters.example: A mixture of 2 kmol N2 and 3 kmol O2 occupies 0.5 m³ at 300 K. Take R_u = 8.314 kPa m³/kmolK, M_N2 = 28 kg/kmol, M_O2 = 32 kg/kmol. Find total pressure, partial pressures, mole fractions and R_mix. Answer: n = 5 kmol, p = 24.9 MPa, y_N2 = 0.4, y_O2 = 0.6, p_N2 = 9.98 MPa, p_O2 = 15.0 MPa, M_mix = 30.4 kg/kmol, R_mix = 0.273 kJ/kgK.
chapters.trap: Using mass fractions in place of mole fractions in Dalton's law. Partial pressure uses the mixture volume and temperature, not the component's own volume.
chapters.prereq: 5.7 ideal gas law; Unit 1 pressure and mole concept.
chapters.leave: Real gas mixture EOS and chemical potential go to advanced courses; the psychrometric mixture of dry air and water vapour goes to 5.10.

chapters.idea: Moist air is a mixture of dry air and water vapour; humidity ratios and the psychrometric chart fix its state for heating, cooling and drying.
chapters.depth: Define dry-bulb temperature, wet-bulb temperature, dew point, relative humidity φ = p_v/p_sat(T), humidity ratio w = 0.622 p_v/(p - p_v) for air-water vapour, and enthalpy of moist air. Show the saturation curve and constant RH lines on the chart conceptually. Use Dalton's law from 5.9. Some syllabi list psychrometry in the refrigeration unit.

figure.aria: A psychrometric plot shows the saturation humidity ratio rising with dry-bulb temperature and a state point at 30 degrees Celsius and 0.0160 kilograms of water vapour per kilogram of dry air.

chapters.example: Moist air at 30°C dry-bulb and 60% relative humidity at 101.325 kPa. Saturation pressure at 30°C is 4.246 kPa. Find vapour pressure, humidity ratio and dew point. Answer: p_v = 2.548 kPa, w = 0.0160 kg/kg dry air, dew point ≈ 21.3°C.
chapters.trap: Using total pressure in place of dry-air pressure in w, or confusing relative humidity with humidity ratio. Wet-bulb and dew point are not the same.
chapters.prereq: 5.9 Dalton partial pressure; 5.5 steam table saturation pressure.
chapters.leave: Air-conditioning load, coil and cooling-tower design go to later refrigeration or air-conditioning courses; real moist-air corrections are advanced.
